name: Density (density-rs)
workload: In-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes), single thread, lzbench 2.4.
claimed_speedup: Compression 1630 MB/s at ratio 62.77% (density 0.16.6 -1) versus lz4 1.10.0 --fast -17 at 924 MB/s and 62.15%, and lz4 default at 550 MB/s and 47.60%; Snappy 1.3.1 457 MB/s at 47.85%. Compression about 1.8x lz4 --fast -17 (derived from page data). Decompression 1617 MB/s versus lz4 3832-3977 MB/s, so slower than lz4 on decode.
compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0, options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4, silesia.tar; per-codec compile flags are in the lzbench Makefile, not on the results page; density is built by lzbench through the Rust toolchain
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
tradeoffs: Ratio is far worse than lz4 default (62.77% versus 47.60% of original size at level 1); the three algorithms (chameleon, cheetah, lion) trade ratio for speed. Rewritten from the original C99 library into Rust; the page opened shows only Cargo usage, and the latest commits mention C bindings.
caveats: Win is compression speed only; decompression is about 2.4x slower than lz4 on the same table. The README's own pareto-frontier claim points to a squash-benchmark page on github.io that could not be opened (egress blocked). Not-default lz4 level used for the like-for-like ratio comparison. Build flags for the Rust codec inside lzbench are not stated.

name: LZFSE
workload: In-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes), single thread, lzbench 2.4.
claimed_speedup: lzfse 91.1 MB/s compress, 732 MB/s decompress, ratio 31.91% versus zlib 1.3.2 -6 at 26.8 MB/s, 314 MB/s, 32.19%: about 3.4x faster compression and 2.3x faster decompression at similar ratio (derived from page data). Repo README states the algorithm targets similar compression rates at higher compression and decompression speed than deflate using zlib.
compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0, options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4, silesia.tar; per-codec compile flags are in the lzbench Makefile, not on the results page
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; shipped in Apple's Compression framework
tradeoffs: Reference C implementation of Apple's LZ + finite state entropy codec; lzvn variant is faster but weaker. Not streaming-focused.
caveats: In the same lzbench table libdeflate 1.26 -6 reaches 82.1 MB/s compress and 820 MB/s decompress at 31.85%, so LZFSE beats zlib but not libdeflate on decode and trails it on ratio. Repo is frozen since 2017 (last commit a merge of a documentation pull request).

name: libbsc
workload: In-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar (211,947,520 bytes), single thread, lzbench 2.4; BWT codec at ratio near xz.
claimed_speedup: bsc 3.3.12 -m0 -e1: 19.4 MB/s compress at ratio 23.26% versus xz 5.8.4 -5 at 3.84 MB/s and 23.70%, and xz -9 at 2.75 MB/s and 23.01%: about 5x faster compression than xz -5 at slightly smaller output (derived from page data).

The libbsc README has no benchmark numbers, so all evidence comes from the lzbench table. lzbench notes bsc multithreaded decompress faults on 32-bit ARM. Whether bsc used internal threads in the single-thread lzbench run is not stated.

name: libzling
workload: Compression of enwik8 (100,000,000 bytes) in the README, and silesia.tar in lzbench 2.4.
claimed_speedup: README: libzling e0 encodes enwik8 in 2.208 s versus gzip 6.502 s (about 2.9x, derived from page data) with output 31,456,189 versus 36,518,322 bytes; README headline says 3 times as fast as gzip on compressing with much better ratio and decompression speed. lzbench 2.4: zling -0 86.1 MB/s compress at 29.72% versus zlib 1.3.2 -6 at 26.8 MB/s and 32.19% (about 3.2x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0, options -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4, silesia.tar; per-codec compile flags are in the lzbench Makefile, not on the results page; README sample builds with g++ -O3
hardware: AMD EPYC 9555P 3.20 GHz, single thread, performance governor, turbo disabled, Ubuntu 26.04; README run on Intel Xeon E5-2620 v3 2.40 GHz, Linux 2.6.32
tradeoffs: Order-1 ROLZ with Huffman coding; 16 MB blocks. Compression ratio beats zlib and approaches bzip2.
caveats: Decompression in lzbench is slower than zlib (183 MB/s versus 314 MB/s at -6), though the README shows slightly faster decode than gzip on enwik8. Repo archived 2021-04-26 and points to richox/orz as successor. License is the BSD-3-Clause text in source headers; there is no LICENSE file.

claimed_speedup: Compresses at about 180 MB/s or more and decompresses at about 300 MB/s, typically 5x faster than zlib, with about 30% fewer bytes than other high-speed libraries for text.

name: ACEAPEX
workload: Decompression of a 1 GB FASTQ file (ERR194147) and enwik9 and silesia, lzbench 2.3, host-to-host.
claimed_speedup: FASTQ 1 GB: ACEAPEX -T8 decodes at 7,401 MB/s versus zstd -3 at 2,026 MB/s at comparable ratio (3.98 versus 3.96), 3.65x faster; enwik9 5,109 MB/s and silesia 5,594 MB/s with 8 threads; 1-thread CPU 1,624 MB/s on FASTQ.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -std=c++17 (README build line); libzstd 1.4.8 for the zstd comparison
hardware: Not stated for the headline table; one verify log mentions an EPYC 4344P
tradeoffs: Block-local match search gives independent block decode, parallel and GPU decode, and random access; ratio is below zstd -19 (README says zstd -19 is 1.2-1.55x denser on FASTQ). Encode is slow (about 340 MB/s on 50 GB, 270 MB/s on chr1 with 8 threads). Mode 2 GPU path needs closed-source nvCOMP.
caveats: Headline win compares 8-thread ACEAPEX decode against zstd decode that is presumably single-threaded, and is targeted at genomic data. In the independent lzbench 2.4 table on silesia.tar, single-thread aceapex 1.0.1 decodes at only 675-679 MB/s versus zstd 1.5.7 -1 at 1351 MB/s, with compression at 55.9 MB/s versus 411 MB/s, so on general data it is not faster than zstd. The repo is days old (about 40 commits per day visible, 642 total) and an earlier published figure was corrected after a bad sample file. Format 2 in the repo differs from the format 1 in lzbench.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): lzbench README 2.4 table (aceapex 1.0.1 rows); TurboBench codec list (aceapex added 2026/10)

name: AOCL-Compression
workload: Single-core in-memory compression of the Silesia tar (211,957,760 bytes) through lzbench, AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370, boost disabled.
claimed_speedup: Level 9: aocl-zlib 27.47 MB/s compress, 439.38 MB/s decompress, ratio 32.21% versus zlib 1.3.2 7.37 MB/s, 212.55 MB/s, 31.91% (about 3.7x and 2.1x). PR summary: bzip2 2.1-2.3x compress and +60-69% decompress, Snappy +20% compress and 2x decompress, zstd +14-21% compress and +8-10% decompress, lz4 +5% and +2%.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 15.2.0 with lzbench; compile flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370, single core pinned to CPU 0, boost disabled, performance governor
license: BSD-3-Clause (file-by-file: also MIT and NCSA plus upstream zlib, zstd, bzip2 licenses)
tradeoffs: Zen-tuned forks of zlib, bzip2, zstd, lz4, snappy and lzma behind one API, with OpenMP multithreading and optional fast modes that cost ratio; the x86 build uses a dynamic dispatcher.
caveats: Numbers come from a pull request written by the vendor, not a neutral run; the repo README itself carries no numbers. The compress speedup is for level 9 where stock zlib is slow, and aocl-zlib ratio is slightly worse (32.21% versus 31.91%). Not compared against zlib-ng or libdeflate on that page. Gains are smaller (5-21%) on lz4 and zstd. Mixed per-file licenses.

name: Firetrail (formerly skim)
workload: End-to-end CLI runs (file in, file out, warm page cache), single thread, on silesia.tar, HDFS.log, enwik8 and enwik9.
claimed_speedup: Silesia: Firetrail White encodes at 1.67 GB/s and Orange at 1.54 GB/s versus lz4 1.10.0 --fast=20 at 0.98 GB/s and zstd 1.5.7 --fast=5 at 0.69 GB/s; geometric mean over four corpora: White 1.6x faster than lz4 and 2.5x faster than zstd on encode. Orange ratio on silesia 1.54x versus lz4 1.56x. Independent lzbench row for the earlier skim 0.1.0: 2313 MB/s compress, 3500 MB/s decompress, ratio 64.53% versus lz4 --fast -17 at 924 and 3977 MB/s and 62.15%.
tradeoffs: Density-inspired 8-byte word hash with a 512 KB table; ratio is low (1.3-1.5x on silesia). White needs a trained dictionary. Streaming with 15-20 MB RSS. Written in Zig; no C API is mentioned.
caveats: Baselines are non-default fast settings (lz4 --fast=20, zstd --fast=5). lz4 still decodes faster (2.53 GB/s versus 1.89 GB/s White on silesia). enwik8 nearly fits the 96 MB L3, which the author says flatters it. No LICENSE file found in the repo, so code must not be copied. The old skim repo only redirects to Firetrail; the lzbench row is for skim 0.1.0.

name: liblzraven
workload: Decoding 89.7 MiB of OS 27 over-the-air payloads, measured with tools/benchmark.py; also a synthetic corpus on Apple M4 Pro.
claimed_speedup: Decoder throughput 1.96x xz -6 with AVX2 at ratio on par with xz -6 (10 wins, 9 losses, 1 tie); decoder memory 35,336 bytes versus 8.06 MiB for liblzma. Apple M4 Pro NEON: 954 MiB/s versus xz -6 at 328 MiB/s (2.91x).
hardware: Apple M4 Pro for the NEON table; x86 AVX2 machine not named
tradeoffs: Clean-room C11 decoder and encoder of Apple's LZRAVEN codec (LZ + rANS) for OTA payloads; buffer-only, no streaming, no allocation in the decoder. Encoder is slow (about 70 MB/s on redundant data, 4-20 MB/s otherwise).
caveats: First-party, on a niche corpus of OS payloads that compress 29.9x, so the ratio is not general; x86 CPU model and compiler flags are missing. The README admits Apple's own decoder is faster (1333 MiB/s versus 954 MiB/s). The repo calls itself entirely AI-authored. Only one commit was visible, date not obtained. Compared against xz only, not zstd or zlib. TurboBench lists it as an Apple lzraven reimplementation.
